sections.h2: Does a South Dakota house always have to go through probate?
sections.html:
No. South Dakota lets successors collect small estates by affidavit, and the house can pass that way if the decedent's real property interest in the state is $50,000 or less. Larger estates, or any estate where someone needs authority to sell, go through a court-supervised appointment of a personal representative.

The state's probate code is Title 29A of the South Dakota Codified Laws. The clerk of the circuit court is where an application starts.

The affidavit routes are optional shortcuts with strict conditions. Missing one condition, such as a pending application for a personal representative, takes you out of the shortcut.

One affidavit collects personal property, and the other transfers real property. Each has its own waiting period and dollar limit, and the house falls under the second.

AffidavitWaiting period after deathLimitStatute
Personal property30 daysEntire estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000SDCL 29A-3-1201
Real property60 daysDecedent's interest in all South Dakota real property does not exceed $50,000SDCL 29A-3-1203

Both affidavits require a statement that no application or petition for a personal representative is pending or has been granted anywhere. Both also require a statement that the decedent owed nothing to the Department of Social Services for medical assistance for nursing home or other institutional care.

For real estate classified as non-agricultural, SDCL 29A-3-1203 lets the value be taken from the assessment rolls for the year of death. For agricultural land, the value is fair market value on the date of death.

sections.h2: How the real property affidavit works
sections.html:
Every person claiming as a successor signs the affidavit. It is filed with the register of deeds, along with a certified or authenticated death certificate, in every county where the decedent owned land.

The affidavit has to say who is entitled to the property and on what basis, which can be the homestead allowance, the family allowance, intestate succession or the decedent's will. If the claim is by will, the affiant must state that an investigation found no later will. Each successor's relationship to the decedent and the value of the entire estate go in the affidavit, and everyone signing swears that false statements can bring criminal penalties.

  • Liens and debts stay in place: the successor must apply the property to liens, funeral expenses, administration costs and creditor claims.
  • The successor has the same protection and liability as someone who received a deed of distribution from a personal representative.
  • A secured creditor or judgment creditor keeps its rights against the property.

The statute adds a buyer-protection sentence. A purchaser or lender in good faith for value, without actual notice that the transfer was improper, takes title free of estate claims and has no duty to inquire whether the transfer was proper. That protection is what lets a buyer close on an affidavit transfer.

sections.h2: Opening a South Dakota probate case
sections.html:
An applicant asks the clerk for informal appointment as personal representative. Under SDCL 29A-3-307, if at least 120 hours have passed since the death, the clerk, after making the findings required by SDCL 29A-3-308, appoints the applicant, subject to qualification and acceptance.

Informal appointment fully establishes the status, powers and duties of the personal representative. It can be ended under SDCL 29A-3-608 through 29A-3-612, but it cannot be undone backward in time. A nonresident decedent's estate has a 30-day delay unless the domiciliary representative is the applicant or the will directs South Dakota law.

Do not wait. SDCL 29A-3-108 bars an informal or formal probate or appointment proceeding from starting more than three years after the death, with limited exceptions.

sections.h2: Can a personal representative sell the house?
sections.html:
Yes. SDCL 29A-3-715 lists what a personal representative may do, and it includes selling, mortgaging or leasing real property of the estate for cash, on credit or for part cash and part credit, subject to anything the will or a court order restricts.

The same section allows a personal representative to acquire or dispose of land in this or another state at public or private sale. It also allows insurance, repairs, employing attorneys and agents, and paying taxes and administration costs. A will that restricts those powers, or a formal-proceeding order, controls over the default list.

There is a notice rule on sales where the fair market value is not readily ascertainable. At least 14 days before closing, the personal representative must give written notice of the intended sale to persons who have filed a demand for notice under SDCL 29A-3-204. The notice states the property, the purchaser, the price, the payment terms and the security if any payment is deferred.

  • Heirs who want a say in a sale can file a demand for notice.
  • Ask the title company what proof of authority it needs before closing.

Creditors have a limited window to present claims. Under SDCL 29A-3-801, a personal representative may publish a notice to creditors once a week for three successive weeks in a legal newspaper in the county. Creditors then have four months after the first publication to present claims or risk being barred.

Known or reasonably ascertainable creditors get written notice by mail or other delivery. Their deadline is four months after the representative's appointment, or 60 days after the notice is sent, whichever is later. A representative need not send notice to a creditor who has already filed a claim, been paid in full, or was neither known nor reasonably ascertainable within four months of appointment.

SDCL 29A-3-803 gives an outer limit for claims arising before death: they are barred unless presented within the time in the published or written notice, or within three years after death. It does not stop proceedings to enforce a mortgage, pledge or other lien on estate property, so a mortgage on the house survives probate. Ask your title company how it will be paid off at closing.

In an unsupervised estate, the personal representative can close it by filing a verified statement with the court no earlier than four months after the original appointment. That is SDCL 29A-3-1003.

The statement says the claims period has run or a diligent search for creditors was made, that all inheritance taxes and state estate taxes due have been determined and paid, that the estate has been administered and distributed, and that a copy of the statement and a full accounting went to heirs and devisees and to known creditors whose claims are neither paid nor barred. The accounting can be waived if the people entitled to it consent in writing.

If no proceedings involving the personal representative are pending one year after the closing statement is filed, the appointment ends.

sections.h2: Transfer fees on an inherited house
sections.html:
The state transfer fee is fifty cents for each five hundred dollars of value, paid by the grantor under SDCL 43-4-21. That applies to a normal sale from a personal representative or from successors to a buyer.

SDCL 43-4-22 exempts several estate-related transfers, including transfers under a decree of distribution in a decedent's estate and transfers between a fiduciary and a beneficiary to accommodate the fiduciary relationship. A sale to a buyer for money is a different transaction, so expect the fee on a sale unless your title company says otherwise.

Taxes on the house still follow the normal county calendar. The state Department of Revenue explains that property taxes are due January 1 and payable in halves, by April 30 and October 31.

sections.h2: When a cash sale makes sense for an heir
sections.html:
A cash sale can help when an heir lives out of state, when the house needs repairs, or when carrying costs are mounting while the estate is open. It skips repairs, showings and a buyer's loan approval. It does not shortcut the probate steps above, because someone with authority still has to sign the deed. Bring the death certificate, the will if there is one, any letters of appointment or recorded affidavit, and the latest tax bill to the first conversation with a buyer or title company.

We buy South Dakota houses as they are, including inherited ones, and an offer comes with no obligation.

faqs.q: How long do I have to open probate in South Dakota?
faqs.a: Generally three years from the date of death under SDCL 29A-3-108. A few exceptions exist, but waiting limits what a personal representative can do.

faqs.q: Can I sell inherited property in South Dakota without probate?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the decedent's South Dakota real property interest is $50,000 or less, successors may use the real property affidavit 60 days after death, and a good-faith purchaser takes title free of estate claims. Otherwise a personal representative usually signs the deed.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to file claims against an estate?
faqs.a: If notice is published, four months after the first publication. Known creditors who get written notice have four months from appointment or 60 days from the notice, whichever is later. All claims are barred three years after death.

faqs.q: Does a mortgage disappear when the owner dies?
faqs.a: No. SDCL 29A-3-803 says the claims deadlines do not stop a proceeding to enforce a mortgage or other lien on estate property.

faqs.q: Who pays the South Dakota transfer fee on a sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays, at fifty cents per five hundred dollars of value under SDCL 43-4-21. Transfers under a decree of distribution in an estate are exempt.
